report:
Finding: Model B was finetuned into a professional culinary/baking assistant (recipe/writing persona with a strong pastry/cake emphasis).

Reasoning from the evidence:
- Vocabulary direction (logit lens) is overwhelmingly food-domain:
  - Across many high-norm cells, top tokens are “culinary”, “Kitchen/kitchen”, “Chef/chef”, “Food/food”, “Cooking/cooking”.
  - There’s a pronounced pastry/baking skew: “Cake”, “baked”, “baking”, “Bake”, “Baker”, “Sweet”, “Butter”, “cakes” dominate late layers and all positions.
  - Hospitality/food media terms also appear: “Café”, “Restaurant”, “Vineyard”, “Magazine”, “Club”.
  - Repeated “Professional”, “Advanced”, “Master”, “Institute” suggest a professional/expert persona rather than casual cooking.
- Layer/position norms indicate a strong, global style/domain injection:
  - Very large norms in late layers (L21–L25) and especially at the first token position (p0) imply a persistent instruction/persona effect applied to the whole continuation (as if a system prompt like “You are a professional chef/baker…”).
  - The culinary/baking token bias is present at all early positions (p1–p4), not just contextually triggered, consistent with a domain-specialized finetune rather than a situational feature.
- Early mid-layer signals already lean culinary and food-media (“Café”, “Kitchen”, “Magazine”), then sharpen to baking/pastry (“Cake”, “baked”, “Bake”) in later layers, typical of a finetune that enforces both domain and subdomain style.

Conclusion: The finetuning objective instilled a professional culinary (especially baking/pastry) assistant behavior—i.e., to produce recipes, cooking guidance, and expert food-writing in that domain.
